steps.do: Find the existing transition rules in the stylesheet.
Count the disabled attributes already in the markup.
Plan the disabled attribute, not aria-disabled, when the required input is empty.
Plan transition of background-color 200ms ease for the state change.
Confirm the markup file exists before the build stage.

K-021384.example: The Save button gets the disabled attribute when the name input is empty. Its CSS sets transition: background-color 200ms ease, so the color change takes 200ms.
K-021384.check: After build, the grep for transition shows the planned 200ms value, and the plan names the disabled attribute rather than aria-disabled.
traps: A small model uses only aria-disabled, which leaves the button clickable. Use the disabled attribute to block the action.
Do not set the transition above 300ms, because it feels slow for a color change.

steps.do: Create the root navigation file in the Navigation folder.
In AppRootView.swift, read @Environment(\.horizontalSizeClass) and show NavigationSplitView when the value is .regular, otherwise NavigationStack.
Confirm both containers are declared in the Navigation source folder.
Run the root view unit tests on an iPhone simulator.

K-021385.example: On iPad landscape (.regular) AppRootView builds a NavigationSplitView with a sidebar, and on iPhone portrait (.compact) it builds a NavigationStack. The unit test sets the size class to .compact and asserts the root type is NavigationStack.
K-021385.check: The xcodebuild output contains "Test Suite 'AppRootViewTests' passed" and ends with "** TEST SUCCEEDED **".
traps: Small models often read the size class from UIScreen instead of the environment, which ignores Split View.
Do not branch on a hard-coded device name.
Keep one branch per container, never both at once.

steps.do: Create the sidebar file in the Navigation folder.
Attach .navigationSplitViewColumnWidth(min: 200, ideal: 260, max: 320) to the sidebar's root view.
Confirm the modifier appears exactly once in the sources.
Create the UI test folder for the layout tests.
Run the sidebar width UI test on an iPad simulator.
steps.cmd: xcodebuild test -scheme AppNav -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPad Air (5th generation)' -only-testing:AppNavUITests/SidebarWidthTests

K-021386.example: The sidebar is set to min 200, ideal 260, max 320 points. On a 1024pt-wide iPad the UI test reads the sidebar frame width and expects a value between 200 and 320.
K-021386.check: The grep prints one line in SidebarView.swift, and xcodebuild ends with "** TEST SUCCEEDED **" with "Executed 1 test, with 0 failures".
traps: Small models often write .frame(width: 260) on the sidebar, which fights the split view and ignores resizing.
Use navigationSplitViewColumnWidth with min, ideal and max instead.
Do not pass the values as strings.

steps.do: Create the tab root file in the Navigation folder.
Attach .tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable) to the TabView that holds the four Tab items.
Confirm the style is applied in the sources.
Run the tab adaptation UI test on an iPhone simulator.

K-021387.example: MainTabView declares four Tab entries with .sidebarAdaptable. On iPhone the UI test counts four buttons in app.tabBars and expects the count to equal 4.
K-021387.check: The grep prints the line containing .tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable), and xcodebuild reports "Executed 1 test, with 0 failures" and "** TEST SUCCEEDED **".
traps: Small models often build a custom HStack sidebar beside a TabView, which duplicates navigation.
Use the built-in .sidebarAdaptable style instead.
Do not expect a sidebar on iPhone.

steps.do: Create a shared nav button file in the Navigation folder.
Give the button label .frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44) and .contentShape(Rectangle()) so the whole frame is tappable.
Confirm every nav button uses the 44pt frame.
Run the tap target UI test on an iPhone simulator.

K-021388.example: NavIconButton uses minWidth 44 and minHeight 44 for its label. The UI test reads app.buttons['Settings'].frame and expects width >= 44 and height >= 44.
K-021388.check: The grep lists every nav button file with minHeight: 44, and xcodebuild ends with "** TEST SUCCEEDED **" and "Executed 1 test, with 0 failures".
traps: Small models often shrink the icon with .frame(width: 24) and never widen the hit area.
The visible icon can stay small, but the tappable frame must be 44pt.
Do not use 40 or 32 points.

steps.do: Create the nav item file in the Navigation folder.
Read @Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) and switch from HStack to VStack when dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize is true.
Set the booted simulator to the largest accessibility text size.
steps.cmd: xcrun simctl ui booted content_size extra-extra-extra-large

steps.do: Run the Dynamic Type navigation UI test.

K-021389.example: At extra-extra-extra-large NavItemRow switches to a VStack, and the UI test checks that the icon's frame.minY is above the title's frame.minY. The test also checks that the title's frame height is at least 44.
K-021389.check: xcrun prints no error, and xcodebuild ends with "** TEST SUCCEEDED **" with "Executed 1 test, with 0 failures".
traps: Small models often hard-code .font(.system(size: 17)), which ignores the user's text size.
Use semantic fonts such as .font(.body).
Do not compare sizes with a fixed pixel number.

steps.do: Declare one @State path NavigationPath in AppRootView.swift and pass it to both layout branches.
Confirm there is exactly one NavigationPath declaration in the sources.
Create the persistence test file in the UI test folder.
Run the path persistence test, which pushes two screens and rotates the device.
steps.cmd: xcodebuild test -scheme AppNav -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPad Air (5th generation)' -only-testing:AppNavUITests/PathPersistenceTests

K-021390.example: AppRootView keeps one @State var path of NavigationPath. The test pushes two detail screens, sets XCUIDevice.shared.orientation to .landscapeLeft, and expects the path count to stay 2.
K-021390.check: The grep prints one declaration line, and xcodebuild reports "Executed 1 test, with 0 failures" with "** TEST SUCCEEDED **".
traps: Small models often create a new NavigationPath inside each branch, so rotation clears the stack.
Keep the state in one place above the branches.
Do not store the path in a global variable.

steps.do: Find every @State or @AppStorage declaration that holds the selected tab.
Count TabView bindings; the total must be exactly 1.
Plan to keep the single selection @State in the root view and pass it down as a Binding.

K-021391.example: rg finds one line, @State private var selectedTab in Sources/App/RootView.swift, and rg -c reports RootView.swift:1 for the single TabView(selection: $selectedTab) binding.
K-021391.check: The declaration search returns exactly one line, and the TabView binding count totals exactly 1, both in the same root file.
traps: Small models copy selection state into each child view, so tab switches reset or desync.
Using @ObservedObject for a plain tab index recreates the object and can reset the selected tab.

steps.do: Find existing focus and outline rules in the stylesheet.
Find any rule that removes the outline without a replacement.
Decide the ring uses :focus-visible with a 2px solid outline and a 2px offset.
Decide the ring color must reach at least 3:1 contrast against both the field background and the page background, per WCAG 1.4.11.
Record the chosen hex color and its measured contrast in plan.md.

K-021392.example: The planned ring is #1d4ed8 on a #ffffff input background, which gives about 6.7:1. The rule is input:focus-visible with outline 2px solid #1d4ed8 and outline-offset 2px.
K-021392.check: The grep for outline none prints nothing, and the plan lists a contrast number of at least 3:1 for each background.
traps: Removing the outline with outline none and adding nothing leaves keyboard users with no focus indicator.
Using :focus instead of :focus-visible is a choice, but state it in the plan.
A light gray ring on white often falls below 3:1.

steps.do: List every checkbox and radio input in the markup with its line number.
Count the checkbox inputs so the plan covers each one.
Find existing size rules for these controls in the stylesheet.
Decide the minimum target is 24px per WCAG 2.5.8 and the planned target is 44px.
Decide the clickable area comes from the wrapping label, not only the native box.

K-021393.example: Each option is a label with min-height 44px and display flex, which wraps a checkbox and its text. The plan records 44px as the target and 24px as the floor.
K-021393.check: The rg output lists every checkbox and radio, and the planned value in plan.md is at least 24px with 44px as the target.
traps: Sizing only the native input leaves a tiny click area when the label is not clickable.
A value of 1rem is 16px, which is below the 24px floor.
Spacing between targets matters too, so plan gaps as well as sizes.

steps.do: Install the Tailwind forms plugin so the select gets a base reset you can style.
In src/input.css, add the plugin line directly after the Tailwind import line.
Write the select markup using only static utility class names, with no string building.
Build the stylesheet once in minified mode.
Check that the stylesheet byte size stays under the budget.

K-021394.example: A select with class 'w-full rounded-md border-gray-300 py-2 pl-3 pr-10 text-base focus:border-indigo-500 focus:ring-indigo-500' and six options renders with no script. The minified app.css should be under 30000 bytes.
K-021394.check: wc prints a number below 30000 and the build prints no error lines.
traps: Do not add a JavaScript select library when the native element already works.
Do not skip the plugin line, or the select keeps browser default styling.
Do not build class names from variables, because the scanner cannot see them.

steps.do: Define each select variant as a full literal class string in one lookup object outside the component.
Search src for an interpolated color class prefix, which the scanner cannot detect.
Build the minified stylesheet.
Confirm that a literal error variant class made it into the output.
Confirm that the component reads the lookup object for every state.

K-021395.example: const variants = { error: 'border-red-500 focus:ring-red-500', ok: 'border-green-500 focus:ring-green-500' } feeds className={variants[state]} on a select. The grep -c count for border-red-500 is 1 or more in app.css.
K-021395.check: grep -c prints 1 or more, and the rg search prints no lines.
traps: Do not build class names with a template string like border-${color}-500.
Do not split a class into fragments such as 'border-' plus a color name.
Do not rebuild the lookup object inside render, because that adds work on every update.

steps.do: List the directory tree to find folders that hold no template classes.
In src/input.css, add a source line for the component folder and a not-source line for dist.
Run the minified build and read the Done in time from its output.
Confirm that a class used only in src/components still reaches the stylesheet.

K-021396.example: Add @source "../src/**/*.{tsx,html}" and @source not "../dist" to input.css. The build reports Done in 60ms and grep -c finds focus:ring-indigo-500 once.
K-021396.check: The build prints a Done in line under 1000ms, and grep -c prints 1 or more.
traps: Do not exclude src/components, since that hides real classes.
Do not use the v3 content array inside a v4 stylesheet.
Do not treat a fast build as proof, because the grep check is what confirms the classes are there.

steps.do: Inside src/input.css, put the shared select utilities under a components layer in one class named select-base.
Apply the single select-base class to every select element instead of repeating utilities.
Build the minified stylesheet.
Count how many select-base uses appear in the component source.
Confirm that the layer emitted exactly one select-base rule.

K-021397.example: The select-base class sets w-full, rounded-md, border-gray-300, py-2, and pr-10 once inside @layer components. rg -c reports 12 uses across src, and grep -c prints 1 for the .select-base{ rule.
K-021397.check: rg reports the expected count of uses across src files, and grep -c prints 1.
traps: Do not put @apply rules outside a layer, since that can change cascade order.
Do not copy the same utilities onto every select when one class covers them.
Do not rename the class in markup without updating the layer definition.

steps.do: Add content-auto and a fixed intrinsic block size to each option element using arbitrary properties.
Build the minified stylesheet so the arbitrary property rules are emitted.
Confirm that the content-visibility rule exists in the output.
Run the render timing test that asserts the first paint of 1000 options is under 200ms.

K-021398.example: Each li in a 1000-option listbox gets the classes content-auto and [contain-intrinsic-block-size:2.5rem]. The Playwright test passes with the first paint of the list under 200ms.
K-021398.check: grep -c prints 1, and Playwright reports 1 passed.
traps: Do not apply content-visibility to the whole page, which breaks focus and scroll behavior.
Do not omit the intrinsic size, or the scrollbar length jumps as options render.

steps.do: Build the minified stylesheet from the current source.
Read the byte size of the built stylesheet.
Confirm that a utility no source file uses was dropped from the output.
Confirm that a select utility which is used is present in the output.

K-021399.example: The minified app.css measures 18432 bytes with the select styles. grep -c finds 0 matches for divide-y because no source uses it, and 1 match for rounded-md.
K-021399.check: wc prints a number under 30000, grep -c prints 0 for divide-y, and grep -c prints 1 or more for rounded-md.
traps: Do not expect a class to be removed if it appears in a comment or string in src, since the scanner still reads it.
Do not put a v3 purge key in a v4 project, because it does nothing.
Do not compare byte sizes between a minified and an unminified build.

steps.do: Import the generated file lib/l10n/app_localizations.dart in lib/main.dart.
Set localizationsDelegates to AppLocalizations.localizationsDelegates in the MaterialApp constructor.
Set supportedLocales to AppLocalizations.supportedLocales in the MaterialApp constructor.
Count the ARB files to confirm each locale has a generated entry.
Run the analyzer to catch missing imports and wrong names.

K-021400.example: A MaterialApp with localizationsDelegates set to AppLocalizations.localizationsDelegates and supportedLocales set to AppLocalizations.supportedLocales shows the form in German when the device is German. With app_en.arb and app_de.arb present, supportedLocales has two entries.
K-021400.check: find prints two lines, lib/l10n/app_de.arb and lib/l10n/app_en.arb, and flutter analyze prints No issues found!
traps: Listing only AppLocalizations.delegate drops the Material and Cupertino delegates, so built-in widgets such as the date picker and back button fail to load their text.
Hard-coding supportedLocales as a list instead of using the generated list drifts out of sync when a new ARB file is added.

steps.do: In lib/l10n/app_en.arb, add the key passwordMinLengthError with the text Password must be at least {min} characters, and declare min as an int placeholder in its @key metadata.
In lib/l10n/app_de.arb, add the same key with German text that also uses {min}.
Regenerate the localization class.
Confirm the generated method signature in app_localizations.dart.
In the password validator, return l10n.passwordMinLengthError(8) when the value length is less than 8, then run the analyzer.

K-021401.example: The key passwordMinLengthError with an int placeholder named min generates a method passwordMinLengthError(int min). The validator returns l10n.passwordMinLengthError(8) when value.length is less than 8.
K-021401.check: grep prints one line containing String passwordMinLengthError(int min), and flutter analyze prints No issues found!
traps: Writing {min} in the ARB file without declaring the placeholder in @key metadata causes gen-l10n to fail.
Concatenating the number into a string in Dart breaks word order in other languages, so always pass it as a placeholder.

steps.do: Add the intl package to pubspec.yaml if it is not already listed.
Import package:intl/intl.dart in the form file.
Build a NumberFormat.currency with locale set to Localizations.localeOf(context).toString() and symbol set to EUR, and use it only for the display text.
Store the raw double value in the model and never write the formatted string back to the TextEditingController.
Run the locale test that pumps the form in a German locale and checks the displayed amount.

K-021402.example: NumberFormat.currency with locale de_DE and symbol EUR formats 1234.5 as 1.234,50 EUR. The model keeps 1234.5 as a double, and only the read-only label shows the formatted string.
K-021402.check: flutter test test/form_locale_test.dart prints All tests passed! and the assertion for the string 1.234,50 is among the passing checks.
traps: Parsing a German input like 1.234,50 with double.parse fails because the comma is the decimal mark. Parse user input with NumberFormat for the same locale instead.
Using the device locale instead of Localizations.localeOf(context) ignores an in-app language override.

steps.do: Write lib/l10n/app_ar.arb with @@locale set to ar and the key emailLabel set to البريد الإلكتروني.
Replace EdgeInsets.only(left: 16) with EdgeInsetsDirectional.only(start: 16) in the form files.
Replace TextAlign.left with TextAlign.start in the form field styles.
Confirm that no left: values remain in the form folder.
Run the analyzer to check the edited layout code.

K-021403.example: Replacing EdgeInsets.only(left: 16) with EdgeInsetsDirectional.only(start: 16) makes the label padding flip under Arabic. After the change, grep -rn 'left:' lib/form prints no lines.
K-021403.check: grep -rn 'left:' lib/form prints nothing, and flutter analyze prints No issues found!
traps: Keeping EdgeInsets.only with left and right does not flip for Arabic, so the bug appears only in RTL. Testing only in English hides it.
MaterialApp sets the text direction from the locale, so a fixed TextAlign.left still pins text to the wrong side in Arabic.

steps.do: Count the input elements in the page.
Count the label elements in the page.
List each input, select, and textarea with its line number so every field can be matched to a label.
Count the hidden inputs, which need no label and are excluded from the plan.
Run axe against the served page and record the number of label violations. Start a local server on port 8000 first.

K-021404.example: grep reports 7 inputs, 6 labels, and 1 hidden input, so 6 visible fields. axe reports 1 violation for rule label on the zip field. The plan row reads: input id=zip, visible label text ZIP code, with a for attribute matching its id.
K-021404.check: The label count equals the visible input count, for example 6 labels for 6 visible inputs, and axe reports 0 violations for the label rule after the plan is applied.
traps: Counting type=hidden inputs as needing labels inflates the plan.
A wrapping label works without a for attribute, so do not require for on every field.
Do not use aria-label to replace visible label text that says something different.

steps.do: Find any existing error containers and their ids in the markup.
Check that the planned error id email-error does not already exist in the page. Expect 0 before the change.
List every aria-describedby attribute so the new id can be appended to the existing list, not substituted for it.
List every aria-invalid attribute so the script's toggling of it can be checked against the existing markup.
Run a Playwright test that submits an empty email, then checks that aria-invalid is true and aria-describedby contains email-error, and that both clear after a valid value.

K-021405.example: The email input gets aria-describedby set to email-hint email-error, with aria-invalid set to true when the check fails. The error paragraph has id email-error and sits directly after the input. The Playwright test passes with 1 test passed.
K-021405.check: grep prints 0 for the planned id before the change, and the Playwright run reports all tests passed, including the aria-invalid and aria-describedby assertions.
traps: Setting aria-describedby replaces the existing list instead of appending to it.
Reusing an id across two fields breaks the link for one of them.
Marking an error only with a red border or color gives no text for screen reader users.

steps.do: List every input element with its current type and attributes.
Count the inputs that already have an autocomplete attribute.
List the existing autocomplete values with their line numbers so each can be compared with the standard token for its field.
Create the mapping file that will hold one row per personal data field.

Run a Playwright test that fills a test profile and checks that each personal data field receives its value and that the count of autocomplete attributes equals the number of personal data fields, for example 4 of 4.

K-021406.example: The email field uses type email with autocomplete email. The postal code field uses type text with autocomplete postal-code, because a number type would drop leading zeros. The Playwright run reports 4 of 4 fields filled and all tests passed.
K-021406.check: The grep count equals the number of personal data fields in the plan, for example 4, the mapping table in plan.md has one row for each of them, and the Playwright autofill test passes.
traps: Inventing autocomplete tokens that are not in the HTML standard means browsers ignore them.
Setting autocomplete off on fields that should autofill blocks helpful input.
Using type number for postal codes strips leading zeros.

steps.do: Find the existing required markers in the markup with their line numbers.
Count the native required attributes already present. Expect this to equal the number of required fields in the plan.
Count any aria-required attributes that duplicate a native required attribute. Expect 0 when native attributes are used.
Count the labels that already include the text (required) so the planned labels can be checked against it.
Run a Playwright test that submits the form empty and checks that each required field is marked required and that the sentence explaining the (required) marker is visible.

K-021407.example: The name label reads Name (required) and the input has id name with the required attribute. A line above the form reads: Fields marked (required) must be filled in. grep reports 3 native required attributes and 0 aria-required attributes, and the Playwright test passes.
K-021407.check: The grep for the native required attribute matches the number of required fields in the plan, for example 3 of 3, the aria-required count is 0, and the Playwright required test reports all tests passed.
traps: Relying only on a red asterisk leaves the requirement invisible to people who cannot see color.
Adding aria-required beside a native required attribute is redundant.
Forgetting the required attribute on a field that the plan lists leaves it unenforced.

steps.do: Find existing axis interval or label settings that control how many labels appear.
Write label limits in the plan: compact shows at most 4 x-axis labels, medium at most 8, expanded at most 12.
Confirm the plan names all three counts.

K-021408.example: The plan sets compact to 4 labels, so a 320 px wide chart shows labels spaced 80 px apart. The grep count of 3 confirms each limit appears in the plan.
K-021408.check: The interval grep lists each existing setting with its file and line, and the count command prints 3 or more.
traps: A small model may write fewer labels without a number, which cannot be tested.
Always state an exact count per mode.

steps.do: Find Row and Column layouts that place a chart beside other widgets.
Find screen-size reads that would give the wrong width inside a split pane.
Write the decision in the plan: the chart reads constraints.maxWidth from LayoutBuilder, not the screen size.
Run the analyzer on the widgets folder to get a baseline before changes.

K-021409.example: home.dart places the chart in a Row beside a 280 px sidebar, so MediaQuery reports the full 412 px screen while the chart gets only 132 px. The plan uses LayoutBuilder constraints.maxWidth, which reports the 132 px the chart actually gets.
K-021409.check: flutter analyze prints No issues found! as the baseline, and the Row grep lists the screens that need LayoutBuilder.
traps: A small model often reads MediaQuery width for a chart in a split layout, which draws the chart wider than its space.
Always use LayoutBuilder constraints for chart size.

steps.do: Read the existing select rules in the stylesheet.
Set the target text contrast to at least 4.5:1 against the select background.
Set the target border contrast to at least 3:1 against the page background.
Run axe against the page to list color-contrast violations.
Record the axe result as the baseline before any color change.

K-021410.example: Dark gray #333333 text on white is about 12.6:1, which passes 4.5:1. A #767676 border on white is about 4.5:1, which passes the 3:1 non-text threshold.
K-021410.check: The axe output lists the number of color-contrast violations, and the baseline plan records that number.
traps: Small models often reuse light gray placeholder colors that fail 4.5:1.
Border contrast uses the 3:1 non-text rule, not the 4.5:1 text rule.
Running axe on a file:// path can skip checks, so serve the page over http://localhost first.

steps.do: Find any existing height or min-height rules on select in the stylesheet.
Set the target min-height of the select to 44px.
Set the target font-size of the select to 1rem so it follows browser text settings.
Create the Playwright spec file that will measure the select height.
Run the Playwright spec to confirm the computed height is at least 44px.

K-021411.example: A select with min-height: 44px and font-size: 1rem measures 44px tall in Chromium, so the Playwright check should pass. A select at 32px fails and needs the rule added.
K-021411.check: The Playwright run prints '1 passed' for the height assertion.
traps: Small models set px font sizes, which ignore the user's browser text size preference.
Padding alone does not guarantee 44px height if the line box is smaller, so check the computed value.
Do not hide the native arrow with appearance: none without keeping a visible indicator.

steps.do: Find every outline rule in the stylesheet to see which ones remove focus.
Plan a select:focus-visible rule with outline of 2px solid and outline-offset of 2px.
Set the target focus ring contrast to at least 3:1 against the surrounding background.
Create a plan file that records the focus rule and its contrast target.
Confirm the plan file exists.

K-021412.example: Use select:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #1a4fd6; outline-offset: 2px; } on a white page, where #1a4fd6 is about 6:1 contrast. The rg search should show no outline: none line for select after the change.
K-021412.check: test -f FOCUS.md exits with status 0, and rg -n outline styles.css shows no outline: none line that applies to select.
traps: Small models write outline: none to hide the default ring, which removes focus for keyboard users.
Use :focus-visible instead of :focus so mouse clicks do not show a heavy ring.
A box-shadow ring is also valid, but it is easy to forget in high contrast mode, so check the outline.

steps.do: List the existing test files to see where table snapshots belong.
Confirm the Xcode project has a test target to hold the snapshots.
List the simulator devices available for the test run.
Plan two snapshots per table, one for light mode and one for dark mode.
Set the time limit for each snapshot test at 200ms and the count at two per table.

K-021413.example: InventoryTableSnapshotTests gets testTableLight and testTableDark, each rendered on iPhone 16 and checked against a reference image. The suite must finish each snapshot in under 200ms and produce exactly two images per table.
K-021413.check: find lists the test files, xcodebuild -list shows a test target name, and xcrun simctl lists an iPhone 16 device line.
traps: Do not record only the light snapshot, because dark regressions go unseen.
Do not plan snapshots without fixing the device and scale, since pixels will vary between runs.
A passing snapshot with no reference image proves nothing, so record the reference before the change.

steps.do: Find current hard-coded heights in widget files to see what must change.
Find heights of 400 to 499 px. These are the values that overflow on a 320 px phone and must be replaced.
Check the current chart container for an AspectRatio widget to decide whether ratio or fixed height fits.
Check the per-mode values in the plan: compact 220, medium 300, expanded 360, and legend touch target 48. The count must be 4.
Confirm the Flutter SDK version supports the widgets planned.

K-021414.example: The plan sets compact height to 220 and expanded to 360, and legend touch targets are 48 by 48 logical px. The grep shows one existing SizedBox with height: 400, which is marked for replacement.
K-021414.check: The 4 to 499 grep lists each hard-coded height with file and line number, the value count prints exactly 4, and flutter --version prints a line starting with Flutter 3 or later.
traps: A small model often uses a fixed 400 px height everywhere, which overflows on a 320 px phone.
Pick values per breakpoint and state the logical px unit.

steps.do: List every select element already used in the project's HTML files.
Count how many files contain a select element.
Decide on native select unless the design needs search, typing filters, or multi-column options.
Create a plan file that records the decision.
Confirm the plan file exists.
Run the keyboard test suite for select controls and confirm it reports 0 failed.

K-021415.example: The rg count prints index.html:3 and checkout.html:1, so 4 native selects exist and the plan keeps native select for all of them. Native select already provides keyboard support, the combobox role, and type-ahead without extra ARIA. The Playwright run prints 0 failed.
K-021415.check: test -f PLAN.md exits with status 0 and prints nothing, rg -c prints one count line per file with a non-zero count, and npx playwright test exits with status 0 and reports 0 failed.
traps: Small models build a div with role='listbox' by default, which must then be given keyboard handling by hand.
Do not skip the decision step, because the rest of the plan depends on whether the control is native.
Custom widgets need arrow key, Escape, and Home/End handling that native select already has.

steps.do: Find every select element and its id attribute.
Find every label element that already exists in the same files.
Write a list of selects that have no matching label with for pointing to their id.
Plan to add label for='country' before select id='country' in each missing case.
Count labels after the edits and compare with the count of select elements.
